Evan — thanks for the clear numbers. Below is a technical summary of how Redwood's autoscale / warm-pool and request path map to the SLOs you listed, plus recommended config for a POC.

1) Quick definitions / mechanics- Warm pool: a set of pre-initialized worker instances (model + runtime warmed) that accept requests with <50ms additional setup overhead.- Cold spin-up: provisioning a new instance and loading model weights (~120–180s depending on model and quantization).- Burst capacity (burst nodes): additional instances that can be brought up quickly from warm pool or via accelerated provisioning if pre-warmed capacity is exhausted.

2) Queueing & batching behavior- Requests are routed to a model router that maintains an intake queue with a short batching window (default 200–500ms).- For streaming endpoints, we prioritize issuing the first token as soon as model can produce it: streaming-first scheduling allows the runtime to start token generation even if larger batch is still forming. This minimizes perceived latency for streaming UX.

3) Expected latencies and trade-offs (typical Gen-2 open model on A100-like GPU):- If served from warm worker and with streaming-first scheduling: first-token P50 ~40–120ms, P95 ~220–450ms depending on sequence length and concurrency. End-to-end P95 (streaming start + remainder) typically <=1.2s for avg 60 tokens if warm capacity is sufficient.- If traffic hits cold-start path (no warm workers available): initial requests may see 120–180s delay to finish model load; we avoid exposing this via queueing by holding requests during spin-up and failing over to compatible hosted variants if configured.

4) Autoscale / warm-pool sizing guidance for your pattern- Baseline 20 RPS: 2–3 warm workers (depends on per-worker concurrency tuning).- To handle 250 RPS spikes with P95 <=1.2s and concurrency ~60: recommended warm-pool = 10 workers (this provides headroom for immediate bursts without cold-start).- Warm-pool + burst policy: set burst_capacity = 3x baseline and keep an additional 2 accelerated standbys for very short bursts. That means in practice: 10 warm workers + ability to add 20 more within the burst window.- Scale-up timelines: adding pre-warmed nodes from warm pool is effectively instant (<1s route update); provisioning cold workers is 120–180s. With accelerated provisioning (we can stage kernels/weights on standby SSD) we've observed ~30–60s to bring nodes fully online for many common open models.

5) Queueing & backpressure recommendations- Keep batching window small (200–300ms) for streaming endpoints to avoid delaying first token.- Use streaming-first + prioritized scheduling for interactive sessions.- If you want to strictly avoid first-token >500ms, aim for warm-pool >= 75% of expected peak worker count.

6) Cost considerations- Warm pools increase steady-state cost; we can model this in the MAP. For your traffic, a 10-worker warm pool with burst standby gives strong UX at a modest premium compared to all-cold scaling.

Recommended next steps (technical):
- I'll produce a short MAP slide that maps warm-pool size to expected P95 and estimated monthly cost for your traffic envelope.
- If you can grant a short test token key we can run a staged load test during a scheduled window to validate P95 and warm-pool sizing.
